sections.section_title: Capnocytophaga canimorsus After Dog Bite: Microbiology, Transmission, and the Initial Septic Presentation
sections.description: This section introduces the organism and the clinical context of dog-associated infection, then uses the patient’s first presentation to teach how C. canimorsus sepsis can appear in an immunocompetent adult. It should establish the timeline from bite exposure to fulminant illness and explain why early empiric recognition matters despite delayed culture confirmation.
subtopics: Microbiology of Capnocytophaga canimorsus: gram-negative rod, capsule, fastidious growth, slow culture positivity
Reservoirs and transmission: dog and cat oral flora, bites, scratches, saliva exposure, and close contact
Risk factors for invasive disease and why infection can still occur in previously healthy hosts
Clinical spectrum of human disease: mild local infection, bacteraemia, meningitis, septic shock, DIC, multiorgan failure, and TMA
Case timeline: dog bite to upper lip, lack of early antibiotic initiation, rapid symptom progression over 4 days
Initial presenting features in this patient: high fever, malaise, poor intake, foot discolouration, numbness, and refractory hypoglycaemia
Interpretation of the admission examination and laboratory pattern: sepsis, metabolic acidosis, hyperlactataemia, pancytopenia, coagulopathy, AKI, and liver injury
Immediate differential at presentation: septic DIC, necrotising soft-tissue infection, acute haematologic disease, HLH, and early consideration of HUS
Empiric antimicrobial strategy for dog-bite sepsis, including coverage for Capnocytophaga species
Diagnostic challenges with C. canimorsus and the role of blood cultures versus newer molecular methods

sections.section_title: Early Multiorgan Failure: Sepsis, Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation, and Acute Kidney Injury
sections.description: This section follows the patient through the ICU phase and explains how septic physiology dominated the early course. It should teach the pathophysiology and bedside recognition of DIC, septic AKI, hypoglycaemia, and evolving organ dysfunction, while showing why thrombotic microangiopathy was initially difficult to distinguish from severe sepsis-related complications.
subtopics: Pathophysiology of severe sepsis in C. canimorsus infection
Disseminated intravascular coagulation: consumptive coagulopathy, microthrombosis, bleeding, and ischaemic skin changes
Why pancytopenia can occur in severe infection and how it broadens the differential diagnosis
Sepsis-associated hypoglycaemia: mechanisms, urgency, and differential considerations
Progression from preserved urine output to complete anuria: mechanisms of septic AKI and renal hypoperfusion
ICU management decisions: fluid resuscitation, loop diuretics, blood product support, stress-dose corticosteroids, and close monitoring
Indications for continuous renal replacement therapy in the setting of anuria, fluid overload, and septic cardiomyopathy
Evaluation for alternative causes of the presentation: haematology consultation, flow cytometry, cancelled bone marrow biopsy, ANA and ANCA testing
How DIC-related microthrombotic phenomena can mimic or mask TMA during the early phase
Transition point in the case: resolution of overt sepsis and coagulopathy without recovery of kidney function

sections.section_title: When the Story Changes: Recognizing Thrombotic Microangiopathy and Diagnosing Complement-Mediated HUS
sections.description: This section teaches the diagnostic pivot that occurred after initial improvement from sepsis. It should explain how clinicians recognized a new syndrome—microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia and kidney injury—and how they used laboratory testing, peripheral smear findings, stool studies, ADAMTS13 activity, and kidney biopsy to distinguish CM-HUS from other TMAs and haemolytic disorders.
subtopics: Clinical clue to a superimposed process: sudden isolated fall in haemoglobin without bleeding or haemodynamic instability
Laboratory signature of haemolysis: undetectable haptoglobin, rising LDH, and persistent thrombocytopenia
Direct antiglobulin test interpretation: autoimmune haemolysis versus false-positive results from penicillin exposure or recent transfusions
Peripheral blood smear and the significance of 15%–20% schistocytes in MAHA
Core TMA syndromes in adults: TTP, STEC-HUS, CM-HUS, secondary TMAs, and DIC-associated MAHA
Using PLASMIC score and ADAMTS13 activity to assess for TTP and why an activity of 43.5% argued strongly against it
Ruling out STEC-HUS with clinical history and negative stool PCR for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
Complement testing: what routine C3/C4 and functional pathway assays can and cannot exclude
Kidney biopsy findings in renal TMA: acute tubular necrosis, ischaemic glomeruli, fibrin thrombi, and crescents
CM-HUS as a clinicopathologic diagnosis of exclusion and how the final diagnosis was reached in this case

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of Complement-Mediated HUS and Infection-Triggered Endothelial Injury
sections.description: This section provides the targeted background science needed to understand the diagnosis. It should explain the alternative complement pathway, why CM-HUS develops, how infections act as triggers, and why normal routine complement levels do not exclude disease. The case should be used to illustrate the interaction between host defence against encapsulated bacteria and pathologic complement-mediated endothelial damage.
subtopics: Historical terminology: atypical HUS versus complement-mediated HUS
Alternative complement pathway regulation and the roles of factor H, factor I, factor B, CD46, and terminal complement activation
Mechanism of endothelial injury in CM-HUS: platelet activation, microvascular thrombosis, MAHA, and kidney-predominant damage
Genetic predisposition, incomplete penetrance, and the concept of a triggering 'second hit'
Common triggers of CM-HUS: infections, pregnancy, autoimmune disease, and medications
Why C. canimorsus is a plausible trigger: complement interaction, serum susceptibility, capsule-associated immune evasion, and inflammatory endothelial stress
Why normal C3 and C4 levels do not rule out CM-HUS
Limitations of complement testing after plasma exchange or after starting eculizumab
Interpretation of this patient’s extended complement results, including reduced AH50 and negative genetic testing
How this case fits within the emerging literature on infection-triggered complement-mediated TMA

sections.section_title: Management, Recovery, and Clinical Lessons: From Plasma Exchange to Eculizumab
sections.description: This section explains the therapeutic strategy across the full hospitalization and follow-up period. It should compare supportive care, antibiotics, dialysis, plasma exchange, and complement blockade, emphasizing why eculizumab became the decisive therapy, how infection risk was managed, and what factors shaped prognosis and long-term follow-up.
subtopics: Antibiotic management of confirmed C. canimorsus bacteraemia: empiric therapy, de-escalation, and treatment duration
Supportive management of severe sepsis and organ failure: transfusions, albumin, dialysis, and monitoring of ischaemic complications
Why corticosteroids were started initially and why lack of response argued against autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Role of plasma exchange in suspected TMA: lifesaving in TTP, bridging or temporizing role in CM-HUS, and limitations
Mechanism of action of eculizumab and why early complement blockade improves haematologic and renal outcomes
Therapeutic dilemma of C5 inhibition during or soon after bacteraemia, especially with encapsulated organisms
Vaccination strategy before complement blockade: MenACWY and MenB vaccines, timing limitations, and antimicrobial prophylaxis
Clinical response in this case: return of diuresis, haematologic remission, and partial kidney recovery
Follow-up strategy: maintenance eculizumab, reassessment of discontinuation, renal monitoring, and relapse surveillance
Broader take-home lessons: when to suspect CM-HUS after sepsis, importance of repeated reassessment, and prognosis determinants in TMA-associated AKI
